asic.intro:
A custom AI accelerator (called an ASIC, or XPU) is a chip built for one specific customer's task rather than a general-purpose GPU. Large cloud operators order such chips because, measured against their own workload — usually inference on their own model — they come out 40–65% cheaper than buying GPUs. But the customer does not make the chip itself: design and manufacturing are spread across a long chain of contractors.

How it works. First the specification is fixed: exactly which operation the chip must perform and within what power budget. The chip's behaviour is then described in a specialised language, the logic is assembled from billions of transistors and physically laid out across the die in design software — standard blocks (processor cores, memory controllers, high-speed interfaces) are licensed rather than drawn from scratch. The finished layout is sent to the fab; that step is called tape-out. From it a set of photomasks is made: on a leading-edge node that means dozens of masks costing tens of millions of dollars. The fab then prints the dies, and at final assembly the die is placed on one substrate with HBM memory — without memory sitting close by, the accelerator will not get the bandwidth it needs. To make thousands of such chips compute one model as a single device, high-speed network switches are placed between them.

The most expensive and unrecoverable part is the act of development itself. There is no right to a mistake after tape-out: if a bug is found once it is in silicon, the chip is redesigned and the whole mask set remade — another few months and tens of millions of dollars per cycle. So the bulk of the budget goes not to manufacturing but to design and verification: the one-off development fee (NRE) for a single programme is $100–500M, and the full cycle of bringing out a custom chip costs the customer $2–5B. These costs are fixed — they barely depend on volume. Which means the saving against GPUs only appears at large scale, when the development cost is spread across hundreds of thousands of chips; a custom chip makes sense only for the few whose own demand is measured in gigawatts.

Who pays, and how much. Only five or six cloud operators order custom chips; their combined capex in 2026 is estimated at $660–690B, around 75% of it on AI infrastructure. They pay almost any price for a simple reason: at their query volumes, a 40–65% saving on every workload repays the development in under a year, and dependence on a single GPU supplier is removed. Contracts run years ahead and at gigawatt scale; the largest design contractor alone holds a $73B AI order book, of which about $53B is custom accelerators.

The custom-accelerator market is around $40B in 2026 (estimates range from $13B in 2024 to $150B by 2030). By chip count, custom parts overtake GPUs as early as 2027, but by revenue GPUs stay larger — the difference is price per unit. The design work itself is held by two contractors: one with ~60–85% of the market, the other with ~8–12%.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

asic.problems.items.0.gap: Building your own leading-edge fab costs $20–30B and takes years, and TSMC's 3 nm capacity and CoWoS packaging (chip and memory packaged together) are already contracted out through 2028 — a new player simply gets no allocation. To guarantee itself a place, AWS raised its packaging order by +1,300% at once (from ~5,000 to ~70,000 wafers), directly crowding out others. Until Intel Foundry is running, there is no alternative to TSMC at the leading edge.
asic.problems.items.0.problem: A custom chip can be designed, but there is nowhere to physically manufacture and assemble it. Every leading-edge accelerator is printed by TSMC on the 3 nm node, which in 2026 runs at nearly 100% utilisation against demand roughly three times capacity; then it has to be packaged together with HBM memory (ultra-fast memory next to the chip) using CoWoS (chip and memory on one substrate) — and packaging has become the scarcest link: capacity doubles from ~70K to ~140K wafers a month, while demand is around 1M wafers in 2026. The full cycle from start to first samples takes 18–24 months. Access to a leading-edge fab and to packaging, not the design, is what limits how many custom chips exist at all.
asic.problems.items.0.solution: TSMC is doubling CoWoS capacity (packaging chip and memory together) across 2026–2027 and starts the 2 nm node at the end of 2027 for the next chip generation. A second source is appearing: Google added Intel Foundry as an alternative fab for its TPUs (its own AI accelerators) from 2028 — the first real signal of diversification away from TSMC. New packaging is also developing (hybrid bonding, panel assembly), which takes part of the load off CoWoS. The solution is bringing physical capacity online, so it is stretched over years.
asic.problems.items.0.winners: TSMC captures most of the benefit: near-monopoly control of leading-edge nodes and packaging means it monetises the expansion itself. Broadcom wins second — as the largest design house (chip-design contractor, ~60–85% of the market) it has contracted wafers, HBM (ultra-fast memory) and substrates through FY2028 and gets a priority allocation. Closest to TSMC's quotas are the contractors with privileged access — GUC (affiliated with TSMC) and Alchip (AWS's partner on leading-edge nodes).
asic.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage entrenches today's leaders: the benefit of new capacity goes to TSMC and to Broadcom, which contracted it in advance, and the only door for a new player is Intel Foundry starting up as a second fab.

asic.thesis.bigIdea: The market argues about whose custom chip will beat Nvidia. That is the wrong question. On every custom chip — whoever ordered it — the same narrow circle earns: Broadcom, which designs them, and TSMC, which prints them. And here is the anomaly: Broadcom, the only player with a full stack, is priced like an ordinary semiconductor — not like the owner of the margin that it actually is.
asic.thesis.stream.1.t: Training and running AI models happens on Nvidia's accelerators, and Nvidia sells them at a gross margin of around 75%. For a hyperscaler spending tens of billions a year on chips, that 75% is someone else's profit stacked on top of its own costs. So the largest — Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft — began designing their own chips for their most repetitive, highest-volume workloads. A chip built for a specific workload saves the customer 40–65% of that workload's cost compared with buying GPUs.
asic.thesis.stream.10.t: Hence the industry's central argument: will custom chips kill Nvidia, or will Nvidia crush custom silicon? Companies are valued on the answer to that question.
asic.thesis.stream.11.t: The custom AI chip market by year, $B (spread of forecasts)
asic.thesis.stream.12.t: The numbers say both sides are right at once. By unit count, custom chips overtake GPUs as early as 2027 (~12.5M against ~10.9M) — they grow +45% a year against +16% for GPUs. But in money Nvidia holds ~70–75% of the accelerator market through 2030: its chips cost more per unit. The market is enormous for both.
asic.thesis.stream.13.t: But for an investor, «custom versus Nvidia» is the wrong question. Because the money does not sit in the chip itself.
asic.thesis.stream.14.t: The right question: who earns on every chip
asic.thesis.stream.15.t: Whichever chip wins — Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Meta MTIA, Microsoft Maia — the same narrow circle designs them all. Behind ~60–85% of all custom accelerators stands Broadcom. It is the only one with the full stack: the chip design itself plus the high-speed network that binds thousands of such chips into one cluster (Tomahawk/Jericho switches and SerDes links — the high-speed data lanes between chips).
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.0.label: Broadcom — the full stack (chip + network)
asic.thesis.stream.16.items.1.label: Alchip / GUC / other design services

asic.thesis.stream.16.items.2.label: Marvell — design to order
asic.thesis.stream.17.t: Marvell is the number two (chips for Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia). But the key point: Broadcom gets paid on Google's chip, on Meta's chip and (reportedly) on OpenAI's chip. It does not care which hyperscaler wins the workload war — it collects its cheque from each of them.
asic.thesis.stream.18.note: There are only five customers — but each goes through the same narrow circle of design partners.

asic.thesis.stream.19.t: Why this business cannot be entered
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: precisely what the hyperscalers want to stop paying for
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: an own chip against a GPU on the same workload
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: custom chips as a share of AI-server cost, 2026
asic.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: it was ~15% in 2024 — the share is growing fast
asic.thesis.stream.20.t: The protection rests on two things. First, networking IP. Anyone can draw a chip, but binding thousands of chips into a single cluster without losing speed is something a very narrow circle can do; Broadcom's SerDes lanes are its crown jewel. Second, money and time. One custom programme means $100–500M of unrecoverable development cost (NRE — paid before the first chip exists) and about two years, while the full cycle costs the customer $2–5B.
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: unrecoverable — paid before the first chip exists
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.1.l: the full cycle for the customer
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.1.n: repays in under a year when switching from GPUs
asic.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: plus the queue at the fab
asic.thesis.stream.22.t: So only four or five companies on the planet can afford a custom chip — and all of them go through the same narrow circle of design houses. That concentrates the money rather than spreading it.
asic.thesis.stream.23.t: The real constraint is capacity, not ideas
asic.thesis.stream.24.t: And here is what the «whose chip is better» argument misses entirely: a chip can be designed, but there is nowhere to manufacture it. Every leading-edge accelerator is printed by TSMC on the 3 nm node (a generation of process technology), which in 2026 runs at nearly 100% utilisation against demand roughly three times its capacity. The chip then has to be packaged together with HBM memory (ultra-fast memory sitting next to the chip) using CoWoS (chip and memory on one substrate) — and packaging has become the scarcest link of all.
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.0.n: against demand roughly three times capacity
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.1.n: capacity is doubling — but demand is ~1M wafers
asic.thesis.stream.25.items.2.n: the queue cannot be sped up with money
asic.thesis.stream.26.t: How many custom chips exist at all is decided by access to the fab and to packaging, not by the design. And here Broadcom wins a second time: as the largest design house it has contracted wafers, memory and packaging years ahead. A newcomer simply cannot join the queue.
asic.thesis.stream.27.label: ONE CRACK
asic.thesis.stream.27.t: Google has added Intel Foundry as an alternative fab for its chips from 2028 — the first real signal of a move away from the TSMC monopoly. Worth watching, but the effect is years out.
asic.thesis.stream.29.t: The margin settles everything. It goes to those who own unique IP, not to those who do the work.
asic.thesis.stream.3.t: Why an in-house chip can beat Nvidia at all

asic.thesis.stream.30.items.1.label: Synopsys / Cadence — design software
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.2.label: Broadcom — the AI segment (design + network)
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.3.label: Marvell — design to order
asic.thesis.stream.30.items.4.label: Alchip — pure design service
asic.thesis.stream.30.t: Gross margin by layer of the chain
asic.thesis.stream.31.t: The pure design services (Alchip, GUC) sell engineering hours — a low margin and dependence on a couple of customers (Amazon alone is ~60% of Alchip's revenue). Broadcom sells IP — and keeps the margin.
asic.thesis.stream.32.t: What is priced in — and where the anomaly is
asic.thesis.stream.33.t: Nobody disputes the growth here: Broadcom's order book is $73B, with a target of more than $100B of AI revenue by 2027. The argument is about something else — who keeps the margin once the hyperscalers grow their own teams. And here is the anomaly: Broadcom, the only player with a full stack, trades at just ~20x earnings — like an ordinary semiconductor rather than the owner of the margin. A $1.85T mega cap priced as a middling name.
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.0.n: a $73B order book and a >$100B target by 2027 — cheap for a full stack
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.1.n: the price of flawless execution — on a falling share (down toward ~8%)
asic.thesis.stream.34.items.2.n: the most expensive in the sector — justified only by >50% growth with no stumbles
asic.thesis.stream.35.t: Our read: Broadcom is fair, closer to cheap; its network protects it from insourcing more than the price assumes. Marvell and GUC are the opposite case: their multiples leave no room for a single weak quarter (Alchip has already printed −29% in one).
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.0: A hyperscaler takes a large programme fully in house
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.0.1: The design house loses its richest contract — insourcing is real
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.0: Nvidia's NVLink Fusion connects third-party chips to its network
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.1.1: Broadcom's core IP (the network) is devalued — it becomes a plain contractor
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.0: TSMC and packaging capacity catch demand sharply
asic.thesis.stream.37.rows.2.1: The shortage ends and pricing power falls across the whole chain
asic.thesis.stream.38.t: None of the signals is lit yet: insourcing is moving more slowly than the market fears, and the network remains the thing that cannot be reproduced quickly.
asic.thesis.stream.39.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
asic.thesis.stream.4.t: To understand the bet you have to understand the engineering. Nvidia's GPU is a generalist: it can execute any task, but it pays for that generality in silicon and energy — part of the chip always sits idle on any given workload. A custom chip works from the opposite direction: it hard-wires ONE task (running a specific AI model) and throws away everything that task does not need. For a stable, repetitive workload that yields more computation per watt and per dollar.
asic.thesis.stream.40.t: Technically the sector is moving from a single chip to a whole system. The hyperscalers now design not just the accelerator but the network, the memory and the entire rack around it — vertical integration for control of the whole machine. The next battlefield is not the chip but the chip-to-chip network: whoever binds thousands of accelerators without losing speed holds the cluster's performance. Nvidia understands this and released NVLink Fusion, a technology that lets third-party custom chips connect to its network so it does not lose control of the interconnect. That is exactly where Broadcom's core strength lies (networking IP) — and exactly where its main risk lies too.
asic.thesis.stream.41.t: Where the money is going: hyperscaler capex (~$850B a year) is increasingly flowing into their own silicon. But they are not only paying for chips — they are paying to stake out an ecosystem. Amazon invested ~$8B in Anthropic so it would train models on Trainium. Nvidia invested $2B in Marvell. OpenAI is designing its chip inside Broadcom. Strategic stakes are a way of contracting demand for your own chip in advance.
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.0.n: a growing part flows out of Nvidia purchases and into their own silicon
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.1.n: an investment that locks in demand for the Trainium chip
asic.thesis.stream.42.items.2.n: even Nvidia invests in those who design custom silicon
asic.thesis.stream.43.t: What the hyperscalers are betting on: their own silicon, to escape Nvidia's margin and control their own roadmap — but they still go through Broadcom and TSMC. What the investor should bet on: not guessing whose chip wins, but buying the companies everyone passes through — plus the riskier pure design houses (Alchip, GUC) as leverage on the same trend.
asic.thesis.stream.44.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
asic.thesis.stream.45.t: Custom chips are not a passing fashion but a structural shift: custom silicon's share of an AI server keeps growing, and the hyperscalers will not stop running from Nvidia's margin. But what earns on that shift is not whoever's chip «wins» — it is whoever they all pass through.
asic.thesis.stream.46.t: Compressed into one thought: bet not on the chip but on the toll gate it passes through. Broadcom is the main bet (a full stack, a ~20x starting point that caps the downside, asymmetry to the upside). Marvell and GUC are the same theme but dearer and without a margin of safety. Alchip is, in effect, a bet on one Amazon contract.
asic.thesis.stream.5.t: Take Google's TPU. At its core is a systolic array: a grid of thousands of multipliers through which data flows straight through, rather than running back to memory each time. A neural network is essentially one large matrix multiplication, and here it runs as a continuous stream. A general-purpose GPU computes the same thing but keeps going back to memory — and spends more energy on the same result.
asic.thesis.stream.6.t: But the key is the split between tasks. Training a model is experimental and changeable: there Nvidia's flexibility wins. Inference — running an already-finished model billions of times in response to queries — is a stable, uniform task. That is what pays to hard-wire. And inference is becoming an ever larger share of all AI computation: a model is trained once and answers constantly.
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: a custom chip against a GPU on the same workload — by dropping the unnecessary silicon
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: in a data centre energy is a hard ceiling; the winner is not the fastest chip but the most efficient per watt
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.2.l: a growing share of all AI computation
asic.thesis.stream.7.items.2.n: a stable repetitive workload — the ideal candidate for hard-wiring
asic.thesis.stream.8.t: The flip side is fragility. A hard-wired chip does exactly what it was designed for superbly; if model architectures change noticeably, it has to be redesigned — while Nvidia simply adapts in software. So custom silicon takes not the whole market but its stable, high-volume core — precisely the part where the volume is created. That is what makes the shift structural rather than one-off: the more inference there is, the more hard-wiring there is.
asic.thesis.stream.9.t: The argument the whole market is having
asic.tldr.0: Custom AI chips (ASICs — bespoke chips for a specific task) are the fastest-growing threat to Nvidia's monopoly: their shipments grow ~45% a year against ~16% for ordinary GPUs (TrendForce, January 2026).
asic.tldr.1: Broadcom dominates (~60–85% of the market), with a confirmed $73B order book and a target of >$100B of AI-chip revenue in 2027. Six largest customers: Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and two others.
asic.tldr.2: Two main risks: concentration in 4–6 customers (losing one collapses the shares) and the threat that customers start designing chips in house.
asic.tldr.3: The most reliable positions are with the companies that get paid on every chip produced regardless of who ordered it: Broadcom (P/E ~20x, unique networking IP), and the chip-design software duopoly of Synopsys + Cadence — they earn on any custom chip, whoever ordered it.
asic.unitEconomics.costCurve: The design houses' main cost line is engineering talent, not equipment. Design cost rises with every new node: 2 nm needs more engineers and more trial runs. That raises the entry barrier and strengthens those already working at the leading edge.
asic.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Broadcom AI: ~50–65% (estimate); Marvell: ~52–59%; Alchip: ~24%; Faraday: ~47%. EDA/IP: Synopsys/Cadence ~85–90%, Arm ~95%.
asic.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: NRE per programme: $100–500M; the full cycle for the customer: $2–5B. A custom chip saves the customer 40–65% of a workload's cost against GPUs.
asic.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics are simple: Broadcom and the EDA duopoly capture most of the margin because they own unique IP. The design services (Alchip, GUC) earn less — they sell engineering hours, not IP. For the customer a custom chip is a $2–5B investment that repays in under a year when switching from GPUs.
asic.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: a mature process, in volume production
asic.unitEconomics.yields.1.note: starts 2027; the first runs will carry a high scrap rate
asic.update.bottomLine: The growth is real and confirmed by contracts rather than forecasts. But the shares already reflect it. The entry point is not «buy now at the highs» but «build a position in Broadcom + EDA on a 15–30% correction» (such corrections are normal for this sector), holding MediaTek/Socionext as satellites.

asic.update.summary: The custom AI chip sector is at maximum acceleration: Broadcom reported +143% AI revenue growth, OpenAI unveiled its first in-house chip Jalapeño, and Marvell doubled its number of active programmes. But the shares have already played the story — Marvell rose 251% in a year, then fell 13% in July. The market no longer argues about growth (that is obvious) but about whether the design houses keep their share once the hyperscalers reach the scale that justifies their own teams.
asic.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: If the hyperscalers start designing in house, the binding constraint shifts to the development tools (Synopsys/Cadence — they cannot be replaced) and IP licences (Arm).
asic.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Broadcom: the only design house able to design an accelerator and supply the high-speed network for it at the same time (its own Tomahawk/Jericho switches + SerDes data-transmission technology). Hence ~60–85% of the market.
asic.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Medium for the design houses (their main cost is engineers, not fabs), but the customer pays for the fab: one programme costs $100–500M of NRE plus $2–5B for the full silicon development cycle.
asic.valueCapture.margins.2.source: Alchip ~24%, Faraday ~47% — depends on the NRE share
asic.valueCapture.takeaway: The durable margin belongs to those who own unique IP (Broadcom's networking) and tools (the EDA duopoly) — not to those who simply execute the order. The design services (Alchip, GUC) earn less and depend on a few large customers.
asic.verdict.bear.0: The hyperscalers (the big cloud owners) could take design in house: Google has already added MediaTek and Intel Foundry as alternatives to Broadcom, and Annapurna (Amazon) designs internally.
asic.verdict.bear.1: Nvidia is trying to keep custom chips inside its ecosystem: it invested $2B in Marvell and opened NVLink Fusion (the ultra-fast link between accelerators) to third-party chips — turning the design houses (the chip-design contractors) into dependent suppliers.
asic.verdict.bear.2: Share prices already embed years of flawless growth: Marvell ~67x forward earnings, GUC ~88x. At those multiples even a single lumpy quarter (as at Alchip: −29%) is a collapse.
asic.verdict.bull.0: The growth is confirmed by contracts: Broadcom's $73B order book, of which $53B is custom accelerators (bespoke AI chips), six customers, and a target of >$100B in 2027.
asic.verdict.bull.1: Custom chips are already 40–65% cheaper than GPUs per workload. Midjourney moved to Google's chips and cut its inference bill (the cost of serving queries to the model) from $2.1M to under $700K a month — a 3x saving. That is a decision with no way back.
asic.verdict.bull.2: The companies that earn on every chip win whatever the outcome: Synopsys/Cadence get paid for every project ($8–11B order book), and Arm for every chip produced (royalties +21% a year).
asic.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — the structural growth of custom AI chips: every new hyperscaler ASIC programme extends the demand.
asic.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the hyperscalers keep ordering custom chips from Broadcom and Marvell — or hire their own teams once the volumes justify it?
asic.verdict.sizing: The custom AI chip market: $12–13B (2024) → $30–70B (2026–2027) → >$100B (2030). The range is enormous because analysts count differently — from a narrow «the die only» to a broad «the whole system».
asic.verdict.summary: The growth is among the best in the whole chain, and the protection from competitors is the strongest, thanks to Broadcom and the EDA duopoly (the two makers of chip-design software). But the share prices already embed years of flawless execution: Marvell trades at ~67x forward earnings, GUC at ~88x. Cyclicality is medium — revenue depends on hyperscaler capex (what the big cloud owners spend on hardware) and is lumpy (NRE projects — the one-off chip development fee — start and end unpredictably: Alchip lost 29% of revenue in a quarter). The central question: will the hyperscalers keep outsourcing design — or hire their own teams and do without the middlemen?
asic.whatIsIt: A chip designed for one single task belonging to one specific customer — usually running their own AI model — rather than a general-purpose processor that can do everything. Large cloud owners order such chips because, at their enormous volumes, the computation works out markedly cheaper than buying general-purpose accelerators. The customer does not manufacture the chip itself: a long chain of contractors works on it, from design through to printing at the fab.
hbm.competition.entryBarrier.why: The only contender — China's CXMT — is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and realistically will not reach volume before 2028 — and then mostly for China's domestic market.
hbm.competition.players.0.note: Its share only falls because the market is growing: in money terms the business doubled in a year. ~90% of sales go to Nvidia: a strength and a risk at once.
hbm.competition.players.0.tech: First to every generation; ~70% of HBM4 memory earmarked for Vera Rubin (Nvidia's new accelerators, replacing Blackwell)
hbm.competition.players.1.note: Grew from ~2% to ~21% in three years — the cycle's biggest surprise. The only way to buy HBM on a US exchange.
hbm.competition.players.1.tech: HBM4 has passed qualification; the bottom logic die is made by TSMC
hbm.competition.players.2.note: Missed an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). Coming back: lead supplier to AMD and >60% of the memory for Google's chips.
hbm.competition.players.2.tech: Spent eighteen months failing Nvidia qualification
hbm.competition.switchingCost: To change memory supplier, a customer must pass qualification again — anywhere from several months to eighteen. Until it is passed, no amount of announced capacity earns a dollar. That is why shares move slowly and predictably.
hbm.competition.takeaway: Three split the market, no one can enter, and customers cannot leave quickly — that set-up is what holds prices up. Only one thing to watch: how Nvidia divides its orders among the three at each new generation.
hbm.demand.backlog: SK Hynix holds more orders than it can produce in three years. Micron has ~$100B of contracted future revenue — several years of its revenue.
hbm.demand.contractStructure: Micron: 16 strategic agreements, ~$100B of contracted future revenue, many at a fixed price or with a floor. ~$22B of customer prepayments. Cloud giants sign multi-year contracts with a guaranteed minimum price. A letter of intent with OpenAI (Oct 2025). This is the main evidence that HBM has partly decoupled from the classic memory cycle.
hbm.demand.customerConcentration: Nvidia is ~90% of SK Hynix's sales and the industry's largest buyer. Google is scaling fastest; Amazon and Meta are more cautious. A single Nvidia allocation decision moves all three makers' shares.
hbm.demand.pricing: 2026: HBM3E up ~20% on 2025. For 2027 the makers assume a several-fold price increase. The turning point: in Q1'26 ordinary server memory (DDR5) became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a strong argument for raising HBM prices further.
hbm.demand.soldOut.0.note: all three; Micron covers ~60% of demand
hbm.demand.takeaway: Memory has never had this kind of revenue visibility: years ahead are contracted and prepaid. While the contracts hold, profits are more reliable than the market's habit from past cycles assumes — which is exactly why drawdowns like July's offer an entry point.

hbm.intro:
HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin DRAM dies and mounted on a shared substrate right up against the processor. The binding constraint on a large AI model is not arithmetic speed but the rate at which data arrives: ordinary memory hangs off a narrow bus, centimetres of board traces away, and the processor idles waiting. HBM removes that constraint — data travels over thousands of parallel lines across millimetres, and a single stack delivers more than a terabyte per second. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without HBM.

How it works. Ordinary DRAM dies are first thinned for this: the wafer is ground from the back from roughly 780 down to 30–50 microns, or a tall stack will not fit the package height and will shed heat badly. Thousands of micro-holes are then etched all the way through each thinned die and filled with copper — these are the through-silicon vias (TSVs), vertical wires connecting every layer at once. Then 8, 12 or 16 dies are stacked and bonded: either through micro solder bumps between layers (thermocompression), or, from 16-layer HBM4 onward, copper directly to copper with no gap (hybrid bonding). The stack sits on top of a bottom logic die (the base die), which runs the whole memory and talks to the processor. The finished stack is mounted on a silicon interposer beside the processor, putting memory and processor in one package.

The hard, expensive part here is not the memory cells but assembling the stack without defects and getting the heat out. At 12–16 layers with thousands of connections, one bad die or one unbonded joint kills the entire stack, taking every good layer beneath it with it. The taller the stack, the more tightly hot dies are packed and the harder it is to pull heat out of the middle, so thinning and the bonding method decide directly how many stacks come out good. The spread in stack yield is the main hidden profit lever: Samsung's HBM4 memory yielded only around 50% in early 2026 (nearly every second die scrapped), whereas the leader's proven bonding process loses markedly less. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.

Who pays, and how much. HBM is the most expensive part of an accelerator: a single chip carries 6–8 stacks, and memory accounts for roughly 63% of the cost of a finished AI chip, against only ~13% for the compute die itself (Epoch AI). One HBM4 stack costs ~$500–550, meaning $3–4K of memory in every accelerator; each generation costs more — from ~$200 (HBM3) to $300 (HBM3E) and $500+ (HBM4). Buyers pay without haggling, because without HBM the accelerator simply does not work and the delivery queue is booked years out: cloud giants and accelerator makers prepay to reserve capacity — Micron alone holds ~$22B of customer prepayments and ~$100B of contracted future revenue. The makers, in turn, are putting tens of billions into expansion: SK Hynix has up to $75B of capex through 2028, roughly 80% of it in HBM.

Three makers hold the market: SK Hynix ~56%, Samsung and Micron at roughly ~21% each. The segment itself grows from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028) on Micron's estimate — faster than any other part of memory; demand added +130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

hbm.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: SK Hynix bonds layers with ~20% less scrap and better heat removal, thanks to its proprietary method using Namics' exclusive adhesive. Whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin; the taller the stack, the more that gap matters.

hbm.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: $75B of investment at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. That capital threshold shuts newcomers out, but it also becomes a risk for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Micron holds ~$100B of contracted future revenue and ~$22B of prepayments, many contracts with a price floor. For the first time memory is partly decoupling from the commodity cycle — but 2028 coverage is still only ~40%.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: this is still memory: the product standardises from generation to generation, and in 2027–2028 new fabs from all three plus CXMT arrive at once. In July 2026 the sector already fell >20% on the fear of a turn alone.
hbm.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is real, but this is not subscription software — it is memory. It rests on a combination: Nvidia qualification + defect-free bonding technology + the capital threshold. The one unassailable part is the difficulty of assembling without scrap, where SK Hynix leads. All of it weakens as generations standardise and new capacity arrives by 2028 — hence an honest three for commoditisation.

hbm.problems.items.0.gap: To enter, a supplier must pass Nvidia's qualification from scratch — anywhere from several months to eighteen; Samsung failed it on HBM3E (the previous stacked-memory generation) and lost an entire chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). The only new contender, China's CXMT, is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and will realistically not reach volume before 2028 — mostly for its domestic market. A new memory fab takes 18–36 months, with output no earlier than 2028.
hbm.problems.items.0.problem: HBM output is capped not by the memory wafers themselves but by two final-assembly steps, and both are sold out. First, building a stack of 12–16 dies with thousands of vertical connections through the silicon (TSVs — vertical channels through silicon) at a low scrap rate. Second, mounting the finished stack on a silicon substrate right against the processor (CoWoS packaging — chip and memory on one substrate; only TSMC does it). From the HBM4 generation, the bottom logic die of the chip also goes to TSMC. A single accelerator carries 6–8 stacks worth $3–4K, HBM already takes 22–30% of the whole industry's wafers, 2026 memory is fully sold out and ~90% of 2027 is contracted.
hbm.problems.items.0.solution: This can only be relieved through higher stack yield and assembly throughput, not through new wafer fabs. SK Hynix is first to perfect the layer-bonding process for each generation (for 16-layer HBM4 the industry moves to hybrid bonding — welding dies copper to copper with no gap). TSMC is expanding CoWoS packaging capacity (chip and memory on one substrate) and taking on the HBM4 base die. In parallel, the scarcest link of all is the queue for assembly machines: they are made by Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI), and they are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.problems.items.0.winners: SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) — 56.4% of the market, first to pass qualification each generation, with ~70% of HBM4 memory reserved for Nvidia's new Vera Rubin accelerators; it wins on the best stack yield. TSMC (NYSE: TSM) — holds CoWoS packaging and, from HBM4, makes the logic die, so the next scarce link moves directly to it. Plus Hanmi and Besi: all three makers buy their assembly machines.
hbm.problems.takeaway: Relieving this constraint strengthens the current leaders: what is scarce is precisely SK Hynix's stack yield and TSMC's CoWoS packaging — the things a newcomer cannot replicate. It does not open the door to a new player.

hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: Complements HBM rather than competing with it. Volume production is Micron's (NASDAQ: MU) — the same winner as in HBM: for it this is one more growing product.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Modules of familiar memory (the same kind as in smartphones), but placed right against the processor. They give large capacity markedly cheaper than HBM, but several times slower. Their job is to hold what does not fit in HBM and relieve it on capacity.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: Does not affect the decision on a 2-year horizon. It is being developed by the same Samsung and SK Hynix — for them a far-off option, not a risk of losing the market.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: The idea of building simple computation into the memory chip itself, to move data to the processor less often and save energy. Technically elegant, but the timelines keep slipping by years, the software does not exist, and it is not deployed in real data centres yet.

hbm.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices HBM as ordinary cyclical memory about to collapse. But HBM has quietly decoupled from the commodity cycle: it is sold out years ahead on prepaid contracts with price floors, and its real constraint is not wafers but defect-free assembly yield. So both the high price and the record margin last longer than the market assumes — and the yield leader (SK Hynix) keeps extending its lead.

Over the past two years the value quietly moved from logic to memory: every accelerator carries 6–8 HBM modules worth $3–4K — more than the processor.

The best-protected ways to buy it are the yield leader (SK Hynix) and the only maker available on a US exchange (Micron), for as long as the shortage holds, plus the bonding machines (Hanmi/Besi), which are needed however the shares fall. Samsung is a separate bet on a comeback and a share shift.
hbm.thesis.stream.4.t: HBM is several ordinary memory dies stacked on top of one another and threaded with vertical channels through the silicon (TSVs), so data travels up and down rather than around. The finished stack sits right against the compute chip on a shared substrate. Without it the accelerator «starves»: the compute core idles waiting for data. Each generation costs more than the last: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.thesis.stream.5.t: What the market thinks: «it's memory, it will crash»
hbm.thesis.stream.6.t: Memory has always been a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. The market prices HBM by the same reflex. In July 2026 the makers' shares fell more than 20% — on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.l: earnings is what SK Hynix costs
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: on a record 72% operating margin — the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: on a record quarter — the classic «this is the cycle peak» reaction
hbm.thesis.stream.8.t: Why HBM decoupled from the cycle
hbm.thesis.stream.9.t: But HBM is not traded on an exchange at a spot price the way ordinary memory is. It is contracted years ahead, prepaid, with a price floor, and co-designed with the customer. Commodities do not behave like that.
hbm.tldr.0: The best supply/demand set-up memory has seen in 40 years: three makers share the market (SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%), all of 2026 is sold out, and the market goes from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028), growing ~40% a year.
hbm.tldr.1: The best return-for-risk is SK Hynix (the leader: ~70% of HBM4 supply — the newest generation of this stacked memory — is reserved for Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next accelerator generation, on a 72% operating margin). Micron is the cheapest way in (forward P/E ~12). Hanmi / Besi / TSMC supply the equipment and the final assembly for this link.
hbm.tldr.2: The main risk is cyclicality: memory gets cheaper the moment supply catches demand, and by 2027–2028 all three makers will have finished new fabs. The sector already fell >20% in July 2026. The question is whether multi-year contracts and prepayments hold the price when that new supply arrives.
hbm.unitEconomics.costCurve: SK Hynix produces at the lowest cost and with the least scrap, thanks to its proprietary layer-bonding method: on average ~20% less scrap and better heat removal than the method its competitors at Samsung and Micron use.
hbm.unitEconomics.grossMargin: HBM costs 5–6x more than ordinary memory per gigabyte. The 2026 paradox: ordinary server memory rose so far that it became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a sure sign HBM prices will be raised in 2027.
hbm.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: One multi-layer HBM4 chip costs ~$500–550, and an accelerator carries 6–8 of them (i.e. $3–4K of memory in every chip). Each generation costs more: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.unitEconomics.takeaway: The share of chips assembled defect-free is the main hidden profit lever: whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin. Today that is SK Hynix. The main share-shift scenario is a Samsung breakthrough on scrap; watch its quarterly margin for it.

hbm.update.bottomLine: Not nothing, but not a break either: Hynix's profit was trimmed slightly, efficiency is real, China is coming, capacity is being built — but demand has not broken. What the market re-rated is less the profit than the duration: investors are no longer willing to pay years ahead for peak margins (everyone knows the sector is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first). Only facts will settle the argument — durable orders, prices that hold, and profit. The nearest clean demand signal is TSMC's report; Hynix reports in about two weeks, into an already lowered bar.
hbm.update.headline: Is July's memory panic worth believing?
hbm.update.stories.0.detail: Hynix's Q2 profit guidance came in ~8% below expectations, and 2026–27 estimates were cut 9–11%. But the cause is company-specific: Hynix has more HBM in its revenue mix, and HBM under long contracts rises in price more slowly than ordinary memory, so its average selling price lagged the market. Meanwhile the margin is a record (~75%), profit is up 500% year on year, and by Q3 pricing catches up with the market as HBM4 ships. This is a Hynix quirk, not weak demand.
hbm.update.stories.0.title: SK Hynix's «miss»
hbm.update.stories.1.detail: Nvidia's platforms (Grace Blackwell and the coming Vera Rubin) face a direct competitor for the first time: AMD's Helios rack bets on an HBM4 memory advantage, and Microsoft has joined the project. For the memory makers this is a second large accelerator buyer besides Nvidia — HBM demand stops resting on a single customer and becomes more durable.
hbm.update.stories.1.title: AMD's Helios rack challenges Nvidia through HBM4; Microsoft is a new customer
hbm.update.stories.1.verdict: HBM demand extends beyond Nvidia — a plus for the three
hbm.update.stories.2.detail: Hynix's record $26.5B equity raise pulled in a lot of memory-dedicated capital, leveraged Korean funds amplified the move, and geopolitics added to it. Tellingly, the biggest fallers were the NAND names — the ones least connected to Hynix's issue, to efficiency, or to HBM supply. This looks like an overcrowded position unwinding, not demand breaking.
hbm.update.stories.2.title: The share-price fall itself
hbm.update.stories.3.detail: A startup compressed a model from ~54 to ~3.9 GB — impressive. But in practice it still needs ~9.4 GB of memory (with overhead), and answer quality falls. This continues a years-long compression trend rather than a sudden «HBM is no longer needed». The question is which moves faster: memory saved, or query volume. So far, the cheaper inference gets, the more inference there is. It matters over years, but it is not a reason to cut forecasts now.
hbm.update.stories.3.title: Model compression (efficiency)
hbm.update.stories.3.verdict: the trend is real, but not a collapse
hbm.update.stories.4.detail: ASML (which makes the machines for memory fabs) expects +75% memory revenue this year and +30% machine output by 2027 — the makers are genuinely investing in build-out. But upgrading existing machines adds only ~4.5% of throughput; serious growth takes new fabs, new machines and time. This is the future supply response (2027–28), not July's shock. Good for equipment demand now, but it pressures the duration of the cycle later.
hbm.update.stories.4.title: ASML's equipment signals
hbm.update.stories.4.verdict: supply is growing, but only by 2027–28
hbm.update.stories.5.detail: Two independent research teams, in Korea and Japan, showed new ways to integrate memory that route around HBM's thermal limits. As layer counts rise, pulling heat out of the stack becomes an ever more serious problem and one of the main engineering barriers for HBM4 and the generations after it. This is a question of future chip design, not of current demand.
hbm.update.stories.5.title: New memory architectures against HBM overheating
hbm.update.stories.5.verdict: heat is a growing engineering constraint, not a risk today
hbm.update.summary: Three weeks ago memory was in high demand — now it is being avoided: the leaders are down 20%+ from their late-June highs and ~$1.5T has left semiconductors, while the S&P barely moved. Below: which of July's fears actually change supply and demand, and which only explain the share prices.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: The binding constraint moves to TSMC's fab (NYSE: TSM): from the HBM4 generation the bottom logic die of the chip is made on its capacity, and it is that capacity (plus the defect-free share on new generations) that will be short in the next cycle.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Output is capped not by the wafers themselves but by final assembly of the multi-layer chip: fine-drilling the channels through the layers, the queue for bonding machines, and the share of assembled chips that come out defect-free. The money in that goes to the makers of the assembly machines — Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI).
hbm.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Growth takes enormous capital: $75B at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% of it in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. Good for the equipment suppliers; risky for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.valueCapture.takeaway: The margin sits with the memory makers (70–85%) and in the key assembly constraints. The best-protected ways to buy it: the makers themselves during the short years, plus Hanmi/Besi, whose machines are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply in 2028: the new fabs together (three makers plus China's CXMT) outrun demand growth, and analysts start talking about a «market correction».
hbm.verdict.bear.1: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) breaks the trio's market: its memory passes qualification at a Western giant, its defect-free share rises, and it completes an $8.55B IPO.
hbm.verdict.bear.2: The ordinary memory cycle returns: spot prices turn down, inventories build, and margins come off the 85–92% peak.
hbm.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2028: on the Q3–Q4 2026 calls the makers say «sold out» again, and final chip assembly at TSMC stays short.
hbm.verdict.bull.1: HBM (stacked memory) prices rise several-fold in 2027: visible in contract pricing (TrendForce data) and in the average selling prices the makers disclose in H2 2026.
hbm.verdict.bull.2: HBM profits have decoupled from the old memory cycle: contracted commitments and prepayments keep growing (~$100B at Micron), and the price floors written into contracts hold.
hbm.verdict.horizon: about 2 years — the window of HBM shortage and high prices (2026–2027); by 2027–2028 new fabs catch demand and the cycle turns down.
hbm.verdict.keyQuestion: Will HBM demand absorb the 2027–2028 fabs — or will overbuild collapse prices the way it did in 2018 and 2022?
hbm.verdict.summary: A strong structural story: memory is acutely short, only three companies make it, and demand is contracted years ahead — hence the record prices and margins. But memory carries a built-in risk: by 2027–2028 all three makers (plus the Chinese newcomer CXMT) will have finished new fabs. When that supply arrives and catches demand, memory prices fall and profits with them — that is how every previous cycle ended. Hence a 7, not a 9.
hbm.whatIsIt: Memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin dies and placed right up against the compute chip. A large AI model sits idle not for lack of arithmetic speed but because ordinary memory cannot feed it data fast enough; this stack feeds it through a far wider pipe over a very short distance. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without it — it is the most expensive and the scarcest part of the chip.

ip.picksTakeaway: The core is Cadence and Synopsys: EDA quality, recurring revenue and low cyclicality (the best risk-weighted economics in the link). Rambus is a direct bet on the memory-bandwidth shortage; Arm is the strongest architectural franchise, but sensitive to valuation and to RISC-V pressure. Hold bonding and patents as a small position: BESI has the greatest upside and the greatest risk (adoption in HBM deferred to HBM4E/HBM5), ASMPT is the diversified alternative, Adeia the asymmetric patent bet with lumpy revenue. The key KPI is the shift from pilot-machine orders to volume orders.
ip.thesis.bigIdea: «Licences and bonding» is two different businesses under one heading, and both grow on the same shift: the AI chip has become too big to make in one piece, so it is cut into chiplets and assembled in a stack (3D). The first business is licences on ready-made chip blocks and design software (Cadence, Synopsys, Arm): software-like margins (45%+), recurring revenue, little capital. The second is equipment for hybrid bonding of dies (BESI): maximum operating leverage, but cyclical. The conclusion: hold the quality (Cadence, Synopsys) as the base, and bonding as a high-risk bet — all the more so now that its adoption in HBM has just been pushed back from HBM4 to HBM4E/HBM5.
ip.thesis.stream.1.t: This section brings together two related but economically different businesses. The first is licensing intellectual property for chips: companies sell ready-made chip blocks, interfaces and patents, and charge one-off payments and royalties for them. The second is equipment and patents for hybrid bonding of dies: joining dies vertically at a very fine pitch. Both grow on the same shift — the AI chip has become too big to scale in one piece, so the industry is moving to chiplets, [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] and 3D assembly.
ip.thesis.stream.10.t: But here is the correction the market often misses: hybrid bonding is NOT yet mandatory for HBM. Both Samsung and SK hynix stayed on thermocompression bonding for HBM4, and pushed the switch to hybrid back to 16-layer HBM4E or HBM5. SK hynix is still developing its own MR-MUF technology. The reasons: JEDEC relaxed the package-thickness requirements, and demand for the very tallest stacks turned out weaker than expected. So hybrid bonding is a growing but deferred scenario, not a universal requirement today.

ip.thesis.stream.13.t: Break the link down by economics. The best risk-weighted position is EDA and IP: very high margin, little capital, recurring revenue, low cyclicality. Patent licensing (Adeia) has an extremely high margin once development is paid for, but the revenue is lumpy and tied to deals. Bonding equipment is high-margin but cyclical, with volatile orders; in exchange it carries the maximum operating leverage — the supplier moves from a handful of pilot machines to volume orders without needing fab-scale capital.

ip.thesis.stream.15.t: Why Nvidia will not replace its suppliers
ip.thesis.stream.16.t: Nvidia knows how its chip ought to work, but that does not mean it would build the equipment that assembles it better than anyone else. The competencies are different: Nvidia's are GPU architecture, software and networking; the bonding supplier's are precision mechanics, surface preparation, optics and alignment, yield and contamination control. The equipment has to work not for a single Nvidia design but for different customers, die sizes and materials, at high yield across millions of operations. And the main barrier is qualification: replacing a proven tool means re-tuning the process and going through certification again. Nvidia is better off keeping several suppliers than reproducing the whole precision stack itself.
ip.thesis.stream.18.t: The quality is concentrated in EDA. Cadence: revenue $5.3B (2025), operating margin 45%+, backlog $7.8B; Q2 2026 revenue $1.58B. Synopsys, after buying Ansys, raised its 2026 guidance to roughly $9.67B. Arm, in the year to March 2026: royalties ~$2.61B and licences ~$2.31B, with data-centre royalties doubling. Rambus in Q2 2026: $207M (almost half of it physical chips, which makes it more cyclical). Adeia: $105M in the quarter at a ~60% EBITDA margin, having signed AMD and Microsoft. BESI: €166M of revenue at a 63.9% gross margin; ASMPT around $570M for the quarter.

ip.thesis.stream.20.t: Where it is heading — technology, money and the players' bets
ip.thesis.stream.21.t: Technology. Demand is being pulled by several lines at once. [[hbm|HBM4|decoupled from the cycle]] is moving to a TSMC logic base die on the 3 nm node (first on the Rubin platform), and stacks are growing towards 16 layers and beyond — which needs denser assembly and tighter control. Chiplets are spreading beyond AMD: the UCIe 3.0 die-to-die standard has raised speed to 64 GT/s and is becoming the de facto industry standard (in the ecosystem of Arm, Cadence, Synopsys, Marvell). Beyond that comes 3D assembly of logic on logic and memory on logic, where hybrid bonding is needed most, plus co-packaged optics. Nvidia has already laid out a [[pkg|packaging|became the main event]] roadmap to packages of 14+ reticles and 24 HBM stacks by 2029.
ip.thesis.stream.22.t: Money. Capital is going into packaging in enormous amounts. TSMC has budgeted $52–56B of capex for 2026, of which 10–20% goes to advanced packaging, testing and masks; CoWoS capacity is quadrupling to ~130k wafers a month by the end of 2026, and the Chiayi complex (AP7) will become the largest packaging hub in the world. Large deals are happening too: Synopsys closed its $35B acquisition of Ansys (July 2025), completing a «silicon to systems» link; Applied Materials holds ~9% of BESI as a strategic bet on hybrid bonding.
ip.thesis.stream.23.t: What the players are betting on. The most striking shift is at Arm: in March 2026 it released its first chip of its own (an AGI CPU for data centres) with Meta as lead partner — moving up out of licensing and into finished processors. The others are each on their own link of the complexity chain:

Then come yield problems at fine pitch; customer concentration (only a handful of fabs and memory makers buy the leading-edge machines, and one deferred programme dents a quarter); the cyclicality of packaging capex; the UCIe standard, which can widen the market and devalue part of the interface IP at the same time; RISC-V pressing on Arm from below; export restrictions on EDA and equipment into China; and high valuations — a correct thesis does not pay if the price already assumes flawless execution.

ip.thesis.stream.32.t: AI is shifting the value in chips away from the simple transistor count towards reusable architecture, fast interfaces and physical assembly. The winners are those whose technology has to be used again and again across many competing chips. The IP companies earn on design complexity, the bonding suppliers on manufacturing complexity.
ip.thesis.stream.33.t: In order of preference: Cadence and Synopsys are the quality core (EDA, recurring revenue, low cyclicality). Rambus is a direct bet on the memory-bandwidth shortage. Adeia is an asymmetric bet on bonding patents, but the revenue is lumpy. Arm is the strongest architectural franchise, but the most sensitive to valuation. BESI has the greatest upside from hybrid bonding and the greatest expectations risk, all the more after the move to HBM4E/HBM5; ASMPT is the more diversified and less explosive alternative. Hold the quality as the base and bonding as a small position.
ip.thesis.stream.4.t: Performance used to grow simply through the number of transistors on a single die. That model hit its limits: the maximum area [[litho|lithography|impossible to replicate]] can print; falling yield on large dies; expensive leading-edge nodes; heat; and memory that cannot keep up with compute. The answer is chiplets: the processor is cut into several smaller dies and joined in one package — leading-edge compute dies, cheaper I/O dies, [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] stacks and networking blocks. The complexity does not disappear — it moves out of transistor scaling and into architecture, interfaces and [[pkg|packaging|became the main event]]. That is where the money is made now.
ip.thesis.stream.5.t: IP licences: what is sold, and why buyers do not do it themselves
ip.thesis.stream.6.t: What gets licensed is ready-made, proven blocks: processor architectures and cores, memory controllers and interfaces (DDR/HBM, PCIe, CXL), die-to-die links, packaging patents. Even a hyperscaler designing its own [[asic|custom chip|earns on every chip]] takes the processor core from Arm, the interfaces from Synopsys or Cadence, the memory from Rambus, the bonding patents from Adeia. Doing it in-house means years of development and carrying the risk of a failed tape-out. Licensing economics are like [[eda|software|impossible to route around]]: a one-off payment plus a royalty on every chip, while the next customer adds almost no cost. Hence margins of 45%+ and recurring revenue.

ip.thesis.stream.8.t: Hybrid bonding — and an important correction
ip.thesis.stream.9.t: An ordinary stack of dies is joined with micro solder balls. As the pitch shrinks, the balls run into a limit: too few connections, higher resistance, extra height, heat. Hybrid bonding joins dies directly — copper to copper, without solder — and gives many times more connections in a smaller area. It is the key to 3D assembly: logic on logic and memory on logic.

litho.intro:
Lithography and the related equipment are the machines that physically make every chip. Manufacturing proceeds layer by layer: on each layer, some tools grow ultra-thin films, the lithography tool transfers the transistor pattern onto them with light, others etch away the excess, and inspection systems hunt for defects a few atoms across. A single leading-edge chip goes through these cycles dozens of times. The hardest and most expensive step is lithography in extreme ultraviolet (EUV), and exactly one company in the world makes those machines.

How EUV works. The finer the transistor, the shorter the wavelength of light needed to «print» it: ordinary lithography works at 193 nm, but nodes of 7 nm and below need 13.5 nm — almost 14 times shorter. That light is produced like this: droplets of molten tin are fired into a vacuum chamber tens of thousands of times a second, and each is struck twice by a powerful laser — the first pulse flattens the droplet, the second turns it into plasma, and the plasma radiates the required 13.5 nm. The difficulty is that light of this wavelength is absorbed by almost everything, including air and glass. So the whole system runs in vacuum, and instead of lenses the light is guided by reflection off a set of ultra-smooth mirrors — each loses some of the light, so only a small fraction of the original reaches the wafer. The mirrors are polished to atomic smoothness; a single supplier makes them, exclusively for one lithography-tool maker. Finally the light reflects off a mask carrying the circuit pattern and transfers it onto a silicon wafer coated with a photosensitive layer.

Why one machine costs $200–400M. Behind it sit around 30 years of development and more than $10B of investment, exclusive optics, and a proprietary light source that has to ignite tin tens of thousands of times a second, reliably, for years. The precision is at the limit of physics, and nobody has managed to replicate that combination of mirrors, source and droplet delivery — Canon and Nikon dropped out of the EUV race, and simpler techniques stalled at the previous generation. The next generation with sharper optics (High-NA) already costs $380–400M a machine. No fab prints nodes of 7 nm or below without EUV — which makes this the deepest physical constraint in the whole AI chain.

Who pays, and how much. Demand comes from just five fabs, which account for ~80% of purchases; each has capex of $10–30B, and 70–80% of that money goes to the tools themselves. They pay almost any price, because without a lithography tool a new leading-edge fab simply cannot be built, and the lead time is 12–18 months: a place in the queue matters more than the price. The sole EUV maker's order book stands at around €39B — more than a year of its revenue.

The chip-manufacturing equipment market was around $135B in 2025 (heading toward ~$150B in 2026), and five companies control 56–66% of the total; in EUV lithography the monopoly is single and complete.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

litho.problems.items.0.gap: An EUV machine cannot be replicated: behind it sit ~30 years of development, >$10B of investment, exclusive Zeiss optics and a proprietary light source. Canon and Nikon abandoned EUV development, and China's SMEE is stuck on the older DUV technology (lithography at a longer wavelength, for larger transistors). Even with the money, a competitor is decades behind, while a buyer waits 12–18 months for a finished machine plus up to a year to tune a High-NA one.
litho.problems.items.0.problem: No chip at 7 nm or below can be printed without an EUV tool (the machine that prints a chip's pattern in extreme ultraviolet), and only one company in the world makes it — ASML. In 2026 it ships ~65 systems (+25% on 2025), but demand from the five fabs (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron) grows faster than output. Each machine costs $200M (ordinary EUV) or $380–400M (the new High-NA generation, with sharper optics), and the lead time is 12–18 months. While lithography tools are short, the fabs cannot raise leading-edge chip output — this is the deepest physical constraint in the whole AI chain.
litho.problems.items.0.solution: ASML is expanding EUV production (printing in extreme ultraviolet) by roughly +30% a year and plans to reach a fleet of ~80 systems by 2027; another +30% is under study for 2028. In parallel High-NA EUV is arriving — a new generation with sharper imaging for nodes of 2 nm and below (volume production 2027–2028). The physical ceiling on expansion is not money but cleanroom floor space (dust-free production halls) at the fabs: the market ceiling is estimated at ~$150B in 2026. So the problem is solved by years of planned build-up, not by a fast jump.
litho.problems.items.0.winners: ASML is the sole beneficiary: 100% of the EUV market (printing in extreme ultraviolet) and ~90%+ of all lithography, so any capacity expansion runs only through it. Its exclusive suppliers earn alongside it: Zeiss makes the ultra-smooth optics only for ASML, and the Cymer light source is a division inside ASML. Among the buyers, TSMC gains most — as the largest customer it gets priority access to new machines ahead of its competitors.
litho.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage only strengthens the incumbent monopolist: only ASML can expand EUV output, so all the growth in demand for leading-edge chips converts automatically into its revenue and reinforces a position nobody can contest.

litho.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices chip-making machines, over and over, as an ordinary cyclical business — and sells them off on fear of «peak capex» (the semiconductor index down 20% on record order books). But underneath the sector lies the least reproducible monopoly in technology: no leading-edge chip exists without ASML's EUV machines (which print the finest lines on a chip), and nobody else can build them. Every drawdown in that monopoly has been an entry point, AI lengthens the cycle, and the next-generation machines (High-NA — a still more precise and expensive version of the same tools) extend the monopoly by another decade.
litho.thesis.stream.0.t: The toll gate every chip passes through
litho.thesis.stream.1.t: Every transistor on every leading-edge chip was physically «printed» onto silicon by someone. And the machine that prints the finest lines is made by exactly one company on the planet — ASML. A new fab costs $10–30B, and 70–80% of that is buying machines from a handful of suppliers. A chip can be designed anywhere, but it can only be manufactured by buying equipment from these companies.
litho.thesis.stream.11.t: The margin goes to whoever owns a mandatory step. And the harder the chip, the more steps and checks there are — the market grows by itself. KLA (inspection) and Besi (packaging) are the margin champions (62–65%): the denser the transistors, the more there is to inspect.
litho.thesis.stream.12.t: Who buys — a narrow circle of giants
litho.thesis.stream.13.t: This market has only five serious buyers. TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron account for ~80% of all demand — their capital spending sets the whole sector. Revenue is concentrated but also predictable: these fabs' plans are known years ahead. The main drivers for 2026–2027 are TSMC's move to 2 nm, Intel's to 18A, and SK Hynix scaling [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]]. And the end customer is the data centre: it already takes ~30% of leading-edge wafer consumption.

litho.thesis.stream.15.t: And demand multiplies structurally: [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] consumes 3x more wafers per bit, the new transistor structure (GAA) adds +15–25% process steps, and [[pkg|advanced packaging|became the main event]] grows by more than 50%. Every chip for [[asic|custom AI accelerators|earns on every chip]] passes through these same machines — and needs more of them.
litho.thesis.stream.16.t: The hidden engine: service on the installed base
litho.thesis.stream.17.t: But the most underrated part is not selling machines — it is servicing them. Every machine sold generates income for years: upgrades, spare parts, support. Lam has >100K chambers installed, and ASML's service brings ~€2.76B a quarter — 25–30% of revenue, recurring and high-margin. Service is exactly what smooths the cycle: even when fabs slow their purchases of new machines, the installed ones keep paying.

Lam's quarterly orders are a record $5.84B, and Applied Materials' $7.91B. A single machine costs more with every generation, while the installed base generates service income for years.
litho.thesis.stream.22.t: Operating leverage is high: KLA's operating margin is 43%, Lam's 35%, Applied Materials' 32%. Service is 25–30% of revenue and grows with the number of installed machines, smoothing the cycle. That is how a one-off machine sale turns into a multi-year annuity.
litho.thesis.stream.23.t: What the market thinks: «it's a cycle, and it's at the peak»
litho.thesis.stream.24.t: Equipment has always been a cycle: fabs buy machines in waves, and a peak is followed by an air pocket. In 2022 the shares fell 55–60% (Applied Materials −57%, Lam −59%). The market prices the sector by that reflex. In 2026 the semiconductor index fell 20% from its peak — even as all five leaders reported records: ASML's €39B order book, KLA's 62.6% margin, and AMAT above 50% for the first time in 25 years.

litho.thesis.stream.26.t: Why this is a monopoly, not a cycle
litho.thesis.stream.27.t: But AI lengthens the cycle. Fab programmes run 3–5 years, Applied Materials has 8 quarters of visibility, and ASML's order book is more than a year of revenue. This is not a spot market that collapses overnight.
litho.thesis.stream.28.t: And the main point: every drawdown in this monopoly has historically been an entry point. ASML falling 15–20% is an entry into a business that cannot be reproduced, not a signal to run. A monopoly like this is almost never absolutely cheap. Demand is structural: leading-edge AI chips, more inspection per chip, a rising price per machine with High-NA, and a new equipment market for packaging and HBM.
litho.thesis.stream.29.t: The market is pricing a cyclical semiconductor business. In fact you own a toll gate on all leading-edge computing — with growing service income on top.
litho.thesis.stream.30.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
litho.thesis.stream.31.t: Technically the sector is heading toward still greater complexity, and complexity is the equipment maker's friend. High-NA is entering volume (the next decade's monopoly), transistors of a new structure (GAA) are arriving, and [[pkg|advanced packaging|became the main event]] plus [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] add ~$1B of new equipment market for every 100K wafers a month. Every new turn demands new machines and more inspection.
litho.thesis.stream.32.t: Where the money is going: TSMC, Samsung and Intel queue for the same machines, and their capital spending ($10–30B per fab) flows straight into the big five's order books. A place in the queue cannot be bought: a machine takes months to build, and priority goes to whoever ordered earlier. China is a separate story: export restrictions close leading-edge machines to it (a revenue risk), but at the same time create demand for domestic equipment (which is what NAURA grows on).
litho.thesis.stream.33.t: What the fabs are betting on: staking out machines years ahead — whoever did not join the queue will not build a plant. What the investor should bet on: the toll gates themselves. ASML is the purest (100% of EUV + service + High-NA ahead); KLA and Besi are the margin champions; the inspection and packaging specialists (Camtek, Onto, Nova) are riskier leverage on the same complexity.
litho.thesis.stream.35.t: ASML trades at ~42x earnings — a premium, but one justified by a 100% EUV monopoly. The key observation: drawdowns of 15%+ (as in July 2026) have historically been entry points rather than turns. The market keeps hanging a «cyclical discount» on this monopoly at every downturn — and keeps being wrong.

litho.thesis.stream.4.t: An EUV machine prints a chip's pattern in extreme ultraviolet (13.5 nm wavelength) — light so fine that air and ordinary lenses absorb it. So everything happens in vacuum, and the light is guided not by lenses but by ultra-precise Zeiss mirrors; the light itself is born from tin droplets struck twice in succession by a laser. This is not one instrument but a whole chain of unique technologies that only ASML assembles: Zeiss's optics and Cymer's light source are each a monopoly in their own right.
litho.thesis.stream.40.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
litho.thesis.stream.41.t: Lithography is not a cyclical business but the least reproducible monopoly in technology: no leading-edge chip appears without ASML's EUV machines, and nobody else can build them. The market keeps selling this monopoly as an ordinary cycle at every «peak capex» scare — and keeps being wrong.
litho.thesis.stream.42.t: The conclusion: every 15–20% drawdown has historically been an entry point rather than a turn. ASML is the purest expression of the thesis (100% of EUV, a service annuity, High-NA ahead); KLA and Besi are the margin champions; and the whole big five is a toll gate on the entire AI build-out that cannot be routed around.

litho.thesis.stream.6.t: High-NA is the next rung of the same monopoly: a still harder machine, still more expensive, still further from competitors. It extends ASML's lead by another decade.
litho.thesis.stream.7.t: Not just ASML: five companies, each on its own step
litho.thesis.stream.8.t: Lithography is the most visible barrier but not the only one. Making a chip takes hundreds of steps, and almost every mandatory step has its own dominant company that cannot be skipped.
litho.thesis.stream.9.t: To read the table, a brief word on how a chip is actually made. Ultra-thin films of material are laid onto a silicon wafer layer by layer — that is deposition. The pattern of the future circuit is then «printed» onto them with light (lithography) and everything unwanted is etched away with acid or plasma — that is etch. This repeats dozens of times until a multi-layer structure of billions of transistors has been grown. And before each print the wafer is coated with a photosensitive lacquer — photoresist — which is then developed like photographic film. Each of these steps has its own dominant company:
litho.tldr.0: The chip-manufacturing equipment market grew to a record $135B (2025) and is heading for $145–170B in 2026. AI, HBM memory (ultra-fast memory next to the chip) and advanced packaging are >80% of the growth.

litho.tldr.2: KLA has the best combination of margin (62–63%) and protection: defect inspection is ~57% of the market, seven times its nearest competitor. Its share grows because every new chip generation needs more inspection.
litho.tldr.3: The main risk: China is simultaneously the largest buyer (~40% of the market in 2024, falling toward ~20%) and a growing competitor (NAURA, AMEC and ACM have taken 6.5% of the Chinese market and keep gaining).
litho.unitEconomics.costCurve: R&D is the critical line: ASML spends ~€1.2B/qtr (~13–15% of revenue). The cost of entry: ASML spent >$10B and 30 years creating EUV. Every next generation costs more than the last — which protects the leaders' positions.

litho.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics improve with every generation: the price per machine rises (EUV $200M → High-NA $400M), margins expand (AMAT above 50% for the first time), and the service base generates recurring income. The harder the chips, the more the equipment makers earn.

photonics.intro:
Optics is needed in an AI cluster because copper has physically stopped coping. At 200 Gbit/s per lane an electrical signal on a copper wire decays within tens of centimetres, while servers have to be connected across metres and hundreds of metres. So data inside the cluster is converted into light: it travels through glass fibre with almost no loss and no distance limit. The device that performs that conversion is an optical transceiver; a scale-out network uses about six of them per GPU.

How it works. The signal passes through a chain of physical conversions. First a laser emits a continuous beam of light — made not on silicon but on indium phosphide (InP), because silicon barely emits light at all. A modulator then switches that beam on and off in time with the data bits, up to 200 billion times a second; in an EML design the modulator is built into the laser itself. A silicon-photonic die then combines several light channels of different wavelengths into one fibre. At the far end a photodetector turns the light back into a weak electrical signal, and a separate chip (an optical DSP) cleans it up and reconstructs it. The newest architecture is co-packaged optics: the optics sits right against the switch chip, removing the long electrical path to a pluggable module and saving up to 70% of the transmission energy.

The narrowest and most expensive point is the laser and its yield. Silicon does not emit light by its own physics, so the light source has to be made on indium phosphide wafers — a temperamental material with low yield, and only a handful of fabs worldwide can produce it in volume. Demand for such lasers exceeds supply by roughly 30% (LightCounting), and a production 200 Gbit/s-per-lane laser is essentially available from one supplier today. It is the laser that sets how many transceivers can physically be built: without it the finished silicon photonics, optical DSP and assembly all sit idle. This cannot be relieved quickly — moving from 3-inch InP wafers to 6-inch (4x+ more devices at half the cost per device) takes years of process development, not quarters.

Who pays, and how much. The shortage is so critical that in March 2026 Nvidia invested $2B directly into each of two key laser suppliers ($4B in total) — into light production specifically, not assembly. For the buyers this makes sense: optics is only ~3–5% of a compute node's cost, but without it the expensive GPUs cannot exchange data and sit idle, so lasers are paid for with almost no haggling. The modules themselves get cheaper as volume ramps (800G ~$360–450, 1.6T ~$1,300–1,500), but the value settles in the laser and the optical DSP rather than in assembly, where margins are thin.

The AI optics market: $16.5B (2025) → ~$26B (2026, +60%, LightCounting); the laser shortage is forecast to ease by late 2026 or early 2027.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

photonics.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection rests not on the module but on what is inside it: EML/InP lasers and DSPs are physical and IP bottlenecks that China has not yet reproduced. The rule is simple: own the bottleneck (lasers, DSP), not the box.
